name: Student Self Assessment
title: Student Self Assessment
answer: Student self assessment asks students to judge their own work against clear criteria and set their own goals for improvement, so they take charge of their learning rather than waiting for the teacher to direct it. It matters because students who set specific goals have a concrete reason to revise their work, and because judging their own work builds the judgment they will need as learning decisions are handed over to them.

crumbs.name: Assessment, Data, and the Early Warning System

sections.body: Self assessment is the practice of having students measure their work against clear criteria and then decide what to improve next. It solves the problem of students who do not understand their own progress and therefore depend entirely on the teacher to tell them what is wrong and what to do. When a student names a strength and one thing to improve, the goal belongs to the student rather than to the tool or the teacher. That ownership gives the student a reason to go back and revise. Over time the practice is meant to build the student's own judgment, not just produce a better draft.
sections.heading: The idea

sections.body: A school configured tool can walk a student through self assessment by asking them to compare their work with a rubric, identify strengths, and name one thing to improve. The student sets the goal, not the tool, and the teacher then reviews the goals and helps students pursue them. The text describes this with upper secondary students, and it does not give separate grade band guidance, so the same sequence of compare, identify, and set a goal is the pattern the book sets out. Early on, students may rate their work too high or too low, and comparing their ratings with the teacher's helps them calibrate. This calibration is the point of the practice, because it is how students' judgment develops rather than staying fixed.
sections.heading: How it works in school

sections.body: The book labels this idea with a study finding. In a study with 345 upper secondary students, goal setting based on automated scores produced the largest gains in revision (Jansen et al., 2024). The text explains that students with specific goals had a reason to improve. No other study, figure, or finding is given for self assessment in this passage.
sections.heading: What the evidence says

sections.body: The student sets the goal, not the tool, and the teacher reviews the goals and helps students pursue them, so the decisions about what to work on stay with people. Students may initially rate their work too high or too low, which means their self assessment cannot be trusted on its own at the start. Comparing their ratings with the teacher's is the check that helps them calibrate, so the teacher's judgment remains part of the loop. The text frames self assessment as part of a gradual handoff of learning decisions to students, which implies the handoff is staged rather than immediate. This description is about practice and is not legal advice.
